API 510 inspection records: what the owner-operator must keep

Short answer: API 510 (11th edition, October 2022) requires pressure vessel owner-operators to keep permanent records for the whole service life of each vessel and pressure-relieving device (PRD), plus progressive records that are updated after every inspection. The records must cover four kinds of information: construction and design, inspection history, repairs, alterations and rerating, and any fitness-for-service documentation. Each inspection report must show the date, the next due date, who did the work, the equipment identifier, what was done, and the results.

A retention schedule only works if everyone knows what it is retaining. This section sets out what the current API 510 actually asks for, how it overlaps with OSHA PSM and Canadian provincial rules, and what an NDE report needs to contain to be usable in the owner's record set. Clause references are to the 11th edition. API standards are copyrighted, so the requirements are summarised here in our own words. Check your licensed copy and any addendum for the exact wording (API standards, api.org).

Need NDE reports that drop straight into your vessel files? Ask for an inspection quote within 24 hours.

Permanent and progressive records

API 510 section 7.8.1 makes the owner-operator responsible for two layers of records for every pressure vessel and PRD in scope:

  • Permanent records are kept for the whole service life of the equipment item. These are documents that do not change: the manufacturer's data report, design calculations and nameplate data.
  • Progressive records are updated regularly with new inspection and maintenance history, and with operating information that may affect integrity.

The practical consequence for a retention schedule is that a single blanket retention period (for example "seven years") does not match the code. Construction and design documents must survive as long as the vessel does, and they should transfer with it when it is sold or relocated. Inspection data must be kept at least as long as it is needed to calculate corrosion rates. Long-term rates are calculated from the earliest reliable reading, so discarding old thickness data can make long-term rate calculations impossible.

The four types of information API 510 requires

Section 7.8.2 says vessel and PRD records must contain four types of information relevant to mechanical integrity. The examples below are paraphrased from the code's lists.

Record typeTypical contentsCommon gaps found at audit
Construction and designSerial number or identifier, manufacturer's data reports (e.g. U-1), fabrication and construction drawings, nameplate photo or rubbing, heat treatment charts, design specification data, vessel design calculations, PRD sizing calculationsMissing data reports for older or second-hand vessels; PRD sizing basis never filed
Inspection historyReports and data for each inspection type (internal, external, thickness), inspection recommendations and their disposition, RBI records where RBI is usedRecommendations closed without a recorded reason; thickness data without CML identifiers
Repair, alteration and reratingRepair and alteration forms (API 510 Annex D gives a sample), reports for equipment kept in service with deficiencies or temporary repairs, rerating calculations, new design conditions and evidence of stampingTemporary repairs with no follow-up date; rerates without updated stamping evidence
Fitness-for-serviceDocumentation required by API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 for any FFS assessment performedFFS conclusions filed without the inputs and assumptions

Fitness-for-service assessment is an engineering evaluation the owner commissions under API 579-1/ASME FFS-1. It is not an NDE activity. Where one has been done, its documentation becomes part of the permanent vessel record.

What every inspection report must state

Within the inspection-history category, API 510 is specific. Inspection reports must document:

  1. the date of each inspection and/or examination;
  2. the date of the next scheduled inspection;
  3. the name of the person who performed the inspection and/or examination;
  4. the serial number or other identifier of the equipment;
  5. a description of the inspection and/or examination performed;
  6. the results.

The records should also show the disposition of each inspection recommendation, including why any recommendation was not implemented. For vessels managed by RBI, the code points to API RP 580 for the RBI records.

That list closely matches OSHA's Process Safety Management standard. Under 29 CFR 1910.119(j)(4)(iv), employers must document each inspection and test on process equipment with the date, the name of the person who did it, the serial number or other identifier of the equipment, a description of the inspection or test, and the results. A report built to satisfy API 510 therefore also covers the OSHA documentation elements. The OSHA list does not include the next scheduled date; API 510 adds that.

Operating records, the 90-day rule, and who approves the results

Section 7.8.3 says site operating and maintenance records should also be available to the inspector. These include operating conditions, process upsets that may affect mechanical integrity, and mechanical damage from maintenance. In practice that means integrity operating window (IOW) exceedances, management-of-change (MOC) records and upset logs need to be retrievable alongside the vessel file. The inspection plan requirements in section 5.1 also expect intervals to take account of recent operating history, IOW exceedances and MOC records.

Section 7.8.4 adds a timeliness expectation that many programmes miss. Documented inspection results must be approved by the responsible owner-operator inspector, engineer or qualified designee. They should be entered into the inspection data management system within 90 days of completing the inspection and/or startup. A retention schedule that only addresses how long records are kept, and not how quickly they are filed, does not cover this expectation.

Before any inspection, section 5.3.2 expects inspectors to review the vessel's history: prior results, prior repairs, the current inspection plan and relevant engineering evaluations. Records that cannot be found at the start of a turnaround are, in effect, records the programme does not have.

Records the inspection plan and CML programme depend on

Section 5.1 requires an inspection plan for every vessel and PRD in scope. The plan should define the inspection types, the next date for each, the NDE techniques, the extent and locations of examination, surface preparation, any pressure test requirements, planned repairs, and changes since the last inspection (MOC, IOW exceedances, other deviations). The plan is itself a controlled record and should be readily accessible from the inspection data system.

For thickness data, the 11th edition adds two recording rules:

  • At each examination point, either the thinnest reading or an average of several readings in the area is recorded and used for corrosion rates (5.6.2.4). Use the same convention every time; switching between minimum and average from one survey to the next distorts the rate.
  • CMLs and examination points should be permanently recorded, for example marked on inspection drawings and/or on the vessel, so that later measurements are taken at the same spots (5.6.2.5). The code notes that repeat measurement at the same location improves the accuracy of the calculated rate.

Without those two disciplines, a retained thickness history can technically exist and still be unusable. For how the stored readings become a rate and a date, see corrosion rate calculation: long-term vs short-term and API 510 interval calculation explained.

Examiner, deferral and recommendation records

Several other API 510 requirements generate records that auditors trace:

  • Examiner qualifications (4.5.3). The NDE examiner's employer must keep certification records for its examiners, including the dates and results of qualifications, and make them available to the inspector. The inspector is responsible to the owner-operator for confirming every examiner is qualified for the work. API 510 gives ASNT SNT-TC-1A, ASNT CP-189, CGSB and AWS QC1 as examples of certifications an owner-operator may require. Examiners do not need API 510 certification.
  • Deferrals of inspections, tests and examinations (6.7). A deferral must be documented and approved by the appropriate people, including the owner-operator's inspector and operations management. The vessel or PRD records must be updated with the deferral documentation before the equipment runs past its original due date.
  • Deferral of repair recommendation due dates (6.8). The new date must be documented in the inspection records, with the concurrence of the inspector and the inspection supervisor. Recommendations past due without an approved change are considered overdue.
  • Changed or deleted recommendations (6.9). If an inspector's recommendation is changed or deleted after review, the records must show the reasoning, the date and the name of the reviewer.
  • Repairs and alterations (Section 8). Repairs must be authorised by the inspector before work starts, and alterations and certain repairs also need an engineer's authorisation. Proposed methods, materials, welding procedures and NDE are approved in advance, and the inspector approves the work at hold points and on completion. The authorisations, procedures, NDE results and acceptance all belong in the repair record. Where the jurisdiction requires National Board (NBIC) repair or alteration reporting, those reports are part of the record as well.

For PRD-specific records, see API 510 pressure relief device intervals.

Exploration and production vessels (Section 9)

API 510's Section 9 sets alternative rules for pressure vessels in exploration and production service. Its records provision is lighter. Owner-operators must keep vessel records. Records are preferably kept per individual vessel, but where vessels are grouped into classes the data may be kept by class. Vessel-specific data must still be recorded whenever an individual vessel is inspected, repaired or altered. The code includes a sample inspection record form (Annex C) and a sample alteration or rerating form (Annex D), and recommends including maintenance events that affect integrity. If your fleet includes E&P vessels managed under Section 9, your retention schedule should say so explicitly.

Canada: ABSA AB-506 and provincial record rules

In Alberta, ABSA's AB-506 (Inspection and Servicing Requirements for In-Service Pressure Equipment; Edition 4 was issued in October 2025) requires owners to keep a current inventory of all pressure equipment they own or operate. Owners must also keep equipment records for each item, covering design information, data reports, inspection plans, integrity assessment, repair and alteration records, NDE records, Certificate of Inspection Permits, PRV servicing records and other relevant maintenance and test records. When equipment is sold or leased, the records must go with it, and the acquiring owner must obtain the history and assess the integrity of what it bought. ABSA must be notified of changes in ownership or location for permitted items. The requirement to transfer records on sale is one many US retention schedules do not address. Other provinces (for example, TSSA in Ontario) have their own requirements, so confirm with the regulator where the equipment operates.

In the US, state boiler and pressure vessel laws may set additional reporting and record expectations, especially where the jurisdiction has adopted API 510 or the NBIC for in-service inspection. Confirm with the state chief inspector's office.

What an NDE report must contain to be usable in the owner's record set

From the owner-operator's side, a contractor's NDE report is only useful if it can be filed against the vessel and trended. A practical checklist that maps to the API 510 and OSHA elements above:

  • equipment identifier and serial number exactly as in the owner's register;
  • date(s) of examination and the examiner's name and certification level, traceable to the employer's certification records;
  • procedure number and revision, approved under the employer's written practice by the responsible Level III;
  • instrument, probe and calibration block identifiers, with calibration status;
  • CML or examination-point IDs that match the owner's inspection drawings, with the reading convention (minimum or average) stated;
  • scope actually completed versus scope planned, with any inaccessible areas listed;
  • results presented as data (readings, maps, indications), kept separate from evaluation against API 510. Evaluation is the inspector's job unless the owner-operator has authorised otherwise.

Getting those fields right at the source is far easier than reconstructing them later, and it lets the owner meet the 90-day posting expectation.

API 510 records: frequently asked questions

What are permanent and progressive records in API 510?

Permanent records are kept for the whole service life of the vessel or PRD. Progressive records are updated after each inspection with new inspection, maintenance and operating information that affects integrity.

What must a pressure vessel inspection report include under API 510?

The inspection date, the next scheduled date, the name of the person who performed it, the equipment identifier, a description of the inspection or examination, and the results. The disposition of recommendations should also be recorded.

How long must API 510 inspection records be kept?

Permanent records are kept for the equipment's service life. API 510 does not set a fixed number of years for progressive records. Keep thickness history long enough to support long-term corrosion rates, and follow any longer jurisdictional or contractual requirement.

Does API 510 have a deadline for entering inspection results?

The 11th edition says approved results should be entered into the inspection data management system within 90 days of completing the inspection and/or startup.

How do OSHA 1910.119(j) documentation requirements compare with API 510?

OSHA requires the date, the performer, the equipment identifier, a description and the results for each inspection or test. API 510 asks for the same elements plus the next scheduled inspection date and recommendation dispositions.

Who keeps NDE examiner certification records?

The examiner's employer. API 510 requires them to be available to the inspector, who confirms examiners are qualified for the work.

Do records have to transfer when a vessel is sold?

API 510's permanent-record concept implies they should. In Alberta, AB-506 explicitly requires records to go to the new owner and the new owner to assess integrity.
